# Measure vs Dimension

In a [[star-schema]], a **measure** is a number you aggregate; a **dimension** is a thing you
aggregate *by*. The test is not the data type. It is whether the value describes an entity that
exists independently of the fact, or is itself an observation made at the fact's grain.

A derived number computed from the fact's own measures — a ratio, a moving average, an indicator — is
still a measure. Giving it a dimension table inverts the arrow: the fact would then reference a table
whose rows only exist because the fact does.

## The worked argument

[[data-warehousing-and-business-intelligence]] argues this at length for a technical indicator:

> "It is tempting to give an indicator its own dimension table, with the value and a pair of
> overbought/oversold flags. That inverts the star"
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/docs/star-schema.md, 2026-07-25

The second half of the argument is about thresholds, and it generalises well beyond finance:

> "Storing them would freeze one analyst's convention — 70 and 30 — into the warehouse, so moving the
> threshold would mean rewriting history."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/docs/star-schema.md, 2026-07-25

A stored boolean is a **materialised interpretation**. Change the convention and every historic row
is wrong. The repo's answer is to store the continuous measure on the fact and derive the flags in a
view, where the cut-points are one edit away. The cost is stated rather than hidden: reading a single
day's indicator now takes two joins.

## Two shapes of "derived"

| | Stored on the fact | Derived at read time |
|---|---|---|
| Example here | the indicator value, `DailyRange` as a `PERSISTED` computed column | the overbought/oversold flags, in a view |
| Why | expensive to recompute, convention-free | cheap, and encodes a convention that may change |

The dividing line is whether the value embeds a judgement. Numbers are stored; judgements are
derived. That is the transferable rule.

## The repository contradicts itself

The SQL side ships the argument's winner. The SSAS side ships the loser: `Dim RSI.dim` exists with
`RSIKey`, `IsOverbought`, `IsOversold` and `DateKey` attributes — exactly the design the document
rejects — alongside a second cube built on it. See [[rsi-as-measure-not-dimension]],
[[keep-the-superseded-version-in-tree]] and [[documentation-drift]].
